subject: Mixed
description: Medium-difficulty practice set (20 questions) covering: Biochemistry, Fundamentals of Electro Therapy, General Surgery & Orthopedics, Kinesio Therapeutics, Medicine, OBGY, Pathology & Microbiology, Pharmacology, Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills, Physiology, Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition, Psychiatry, Psychology.

questions.question: The 'blue dot sign' on the scrotum in a boy just before puberty is classically associated with:

options.B: Torsion of a testicular/epididymal appendage (hydatid of Morgagni)

questions.explanation: Torsion of a testicular or epididymal appendage (hydatid of Morgagni) characteristically affects boys just before puberty, and the torted, infarcted appendage may occasionally be visible or palpable through the scrotal skin as a tender bluish nodule — the 'blue dot sign'.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — The Acute Scrotum
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: A disease that was previously known and thought to have been controlled or eradicated, but has now reappeared, is termed:
questions.explanation: An emerging infectious disease is one newly appearing in a population or increasing in incidence/range. If the disease was previously known and thought controlled or eradicated but reappears, it is specifically termed re-emerging.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Epidemiology of Infection — Emerging and Re-emerging Disease
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: A daily, chronic productive cough is described as a fundamental feature of which conditions?
questions.explanation: A chronic productive cough occurring every day is a fundamental feature of chronic bronchitis and bronchiectasis, whereas interstitial lung disease is characteristically associated with a persistent DRY cough.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Cough
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Which of these is a classic feature of a panic attack, as distinguished from generalised anxiety?

options.A: Gradual worsening of mild anxiety over several months
options.B: A sudden, discrete episode of severe anxiety, often beginning unexpectedly 'out of the blue' and lasting only a few minutes
options.C: Anxiety present continuously for years without any discrete episodes
options.D: Anxiety that only occurs during sleep

questions.explanation: Panic disorder is characterised by discrete episodes of acute, severe anxiety that begin suddenly, often 'out of the blue' with no apparent precipitant, and last for a few minutes — quite different from the more continuous, lower-grade anxiety of generalised anxiety disorder.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatoform Disorders — Anxiety Disorder
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: A child injured by a bicycle handlebar to the abdomen is classically at risk of injury to which structures?

options.B: Pancreatic, duodenal, mesenteric, or liver trauma
options.C: The small intestine or lumbar spine only
options.D: Severe crush injury to the chest exclusively

questions.explanation: Handlebar injuries classically cause focal, high-pressure blunt trauma to the upper abdomen, putting the pancreas, duodenum, mesentery, or liver at risk — distinct from lap belt injuries (small intestine/lumbar spine) or straddle injuries (urethra/pelvis).
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Paediatric Trauma, Patterns of Injury
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: In manual muscle testing, the 'break test' is best described as:

options.A: Applying resistance throughout an actively moving joint to see when motion ceases
options.B: Bringing the part to the end of its available range and asking the patient to hold that position while the therapist tries to force ('break') it out of position
options.C: Passively moving a joint until tissue resistance is felt
options.D: Timing how long a muscle can sustain a maximal isometric hold

questions.explanation: The break test — the most commonly used MMT procedure — has the patient hold the end-range test position while the therapist applies gradually increasing resistance, attempting to 'break' the hold. The alternative 'active resistance test' (resisting throughout the motion) requires more skill and is not generally recommended because results are often equivocal.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: In outbreak investigation, a study comparing the recent activities (potential exposures) of affected 'cases' against unaffected 'controls' is called a:
questions.explanation: A case-control study compares the recent activities and potential exposures of affected 'cases' to those of unaffected 'controls', helping to identify the likely source of an outbreak.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Epidemiology of Infection — Outbreaks of Infection
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: For a typical healthy but untrained adult beginning a resistance training program, the recommended training zone (percentage of baseline RM) generally falls between:
questions.explanation: For healthy but untrained adults, a typical training zone falls between 40% and 70% of the baseline RM, with the lower end of the range safer at the start of a program to focus on correct form before progressing intensity.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Training Zone
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: The chronic form of filariasis, characterised by lymphoedema and gross thickening of the skin of the legs/scrotum, is known as:
questions.explanation: Chronic filariasis (caused by Wuchereria bancrofti or Brugia malayi) produces lymphadenopathy, lymphoedema, hydrocele, and elephantiasis — enormous thickening and induration of the skin, resembling the hide of an elephant, due to chronic lymphatic obstruction.
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — Filariasis
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: When faradic-type current is applied directly over an innervated muscle, maximum contraction response is generally obtained by stimulating at the:

options.B: Motor point — where the main nerve enters the muscle (or, for deep muscles, where it emerges from under more superficial muscles)
options.C: Muscle belly midpoint, regardless of nerve entry

questions.explanation: The motor point — the point at which the main nerve supply enters the muscle, or for deeply placed muscles, the point where the nerve emerges from under overlying superficial muscles — is where maximum contraction response is typically obtained with electrical stimulation.
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Effects of Nerve Stimulation
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Why does ischaemia (reduced blood/oxygen supply) lead to cell swelling and damage?

options.A: Ischaemia has no effect on the Na+-K+ pump
options.B: Ischaemia decreases Na+-K+ pump activity, disrupting osmotic equilibrium and allowing the cell to swell
options.C: Ischaemia directly ruptures the cell membrane through mechanical force
options.D: Ischaemia only affects extracellular fluid, never intracellular volume

questions.explanation: The Na+-K+ pump normally keeps osmotic equilibrium by moving positive charge (and effectively solute) out of the cell, counteracting the tendency of intracellular protein anions and other molecules to draw water in and cause swelling. Ischaemia reduces the ATP-dependent pump's activity, disrupting this balance — which is why prolonged cerebral ischaemia, causing cell swelling and damage, is often fatal.
questions.sourceChapter: The Membrane Potentials — Gibbs-Donnan Effect
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: Massive haemoglobin absorption by the renal tubules in severe falciparum malaria produces which complication?
questions.explanation: In falciparum malaria, massive absorption of haemoglobin (released by destroyed red cells) by the renal tubules produces blackwater fever, also called haemoglobinuric nephrosis.
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — Malaria
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: To determine the amino acid composition of a protein, it is first completely hydrolysed. Which method of hydrolysis tends to yield smaller peptides rather than fully free amino acids?
questions.explanation: While acid or alkali treatment can fully hydrolyse a protein down to free amino acids, treatment with enzymes typically results in smaller peptides rather than complete breakdown to individual amino acids, since most proteolytic enzymes have some bond specificity.
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Determination of Primary Structure
questions.subject: Biochemistry

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: In a practical setup for stimulating the quadriceps with a faradic-type current, where is the indifferent (larger) electrode typically placed, per Clayton's described technique?

options.A: Over the femoral nerve in the femoral triangle
options.B: Directly over the motor points of the quadriceps only, with no separate indifferent electrode

questions.explanation: In the classic technique for faradic stimulation of the quadriceps, one electrode and pad is placed over the femoral nerve in the femoral triangle and secured with a sandbag or bandage, while the other (active) electrode pad is placed across the motor points of the quadriceps.
questions.sourceChapter: Stimulation of Muscle Groups — Quadriceps
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Immediately following delivery, the uterine fundus is about 13.5 cm above the symphysis pubis. Over the following days, it decreases in height at approximately what rate, becoming a pelvic organ by the end of the second week?

options.D: It does not decrease until 6 weeks postpartum

questions.explanation: After remaining constant for the first 24 hours, the fundal height decreases by about 1.25 cm every 24 hours, so that the uterus becomes a pelvic organ (no longer palpable abdominally) by the end of the second week postpartum, with involution slowing thereafter until the uterus is near-normal size by 6 weeks.
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Clinical Assessment of Involution
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: Which two limbic system structures are most strongly implicated in the formation of new memories?

options.A: The olfactory bulb and septal nuclei
options.C: The cingulate gyrus and corpus callosum

questions.explanation: Among the limbic system structures (olfactory bulb, septal nuclei, hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate gyrus), the hippocampus and amygdala in particular play a key role in the formation of new memories — as dramatically illustrated by the case of patient H.M., whose bilateral removal of these structures left him unable to form new long-term memories.
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Forebrain: Limbic System
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.question: Although sodium's atomic weight (23) is lower than potassium's (39), Na+ moves through the resting cell membrane with greater difficulty than K+. Why?

options.A: Sodium ions carry a different electrical charge than potassium
options.B: Ions in body fluids are hydrated, and the hydrated Na+ ion is actually larger in radius than the hydrated K+ ion
options.C: Sodium is chemically unable to pass through any biological membrane
options.D: Potassium is not actually present in body fluids at rest

questions.explanation: Ions in solution are hydrated (surrounded by a shell of water molecules). Despite its lower atomic weight, hydrated Na+ has a larger effective radius than hydrated K+, which is a key reason Na+ crosses the resting membrane with more difficulty than K+.
questions.sourceChapter: The Membrane Potentials — Introduction, Size of Hydrated Ions
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: The active coenzyme form of Vitamin B6, closely associated with amino acid metabolism, is:
questions.explanation: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) is the active coenzyme form of vitamin B6, found attached to the epsilon-amino group of lysine in enzymes, and is closely associated with amino acid metabolism — participating in transamination, decarboxylation, deamination, and transsulfuration reactions.
questions.sourceChapter: Vitamins — Vitamin B6, Biochemical Functions
questions.subject: Biochemistry

questions.question: Chronic amoebic ulcers of the colon are classically described by which shape, due to undermining of the ulcer margins by the trophozoite's lytic action?
questions.explanation: Chronic amoebic ulcers are described as 'flask-shaped' because the lytic action of Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites undermines and enlarges the ulcer margins beneath a narrower surface opening, giving it a flask-like profile on cross-section.
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — Amoebiasis
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: Allopurinol reduces uric acid production by acting as a competitive inhibitor of which enzyme?
questions.explanation: Allopurinol competitively inhibits xanthine oxidase, the enzyme that converts hypoxanthine to uric acid, which is why it is used to lower uric acid levels (e.g. in gout).
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology
questions.subject: Pharmacology
